This is a significant win for our infrastructure business and the beginning of a strategic relationship with tremendous potential,” Amon said on Qualcomm’s fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday. The partnership gives Qualcomm a role in powering Starlink Mobile’s upcoming nationwide terrestrial 5G network as the chipmaker expands beyond smartphones. As part of the deal, announced earlier Wednesday, SpaceX plans to deploy tens of thousands of sites. “Under a multi-year agreement, deployment begins in 2027, and it is expected to be one of the largest 5G deployments in the United States,” Amon said. While the rollout starts in 2027, Qualcomm expects revenue to begin appearing toward the end of its fiscal 2027, with the opportunity taking shape more fully the following fiscal year. “You should think about from a financial standpoint, it will start to appear as we exit fiscal 2027. It is more of a fiscal 2028 from a revenue standpoint,” Amon told on the call. Qualcomm will supply chips and foundational software through its Dragonwing infrastructure platforms, supporting the radios and processing equipment behind Starlink’s ground network. “We provide silicon content for radio, including massive MIMO, as well as the accelerator for the digital unit, and we provide software on the Layer 1,” Amon said. Starlink’s radios will use 64 transmit and 64 receive paths. Qualcomm said the tech can improve coverage and help the network carry more traffic over its available airwaves, while its platforms are designed to improve power efficiency. Amon also pointed to opportunities beyond the initial deployment, saying the partnership includes planning for the next generation of wireless. “I think we have seen a lot of trends of technology ranging from Open RAN to AI native as an opportunity to innovate in this space,” he said. The partnership supports SpaceX’s plans to combine ground-based cellular coverage with its satellite network. “Starlink is building the first fully-integrated nationwide satellite and terrestrial network that will keep people connected no matter where they are,” said Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink. SpaceX also agreed last month to acquire Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio, covering up to 14 megahertz of paired airwaves. title: Will Suncor's Refining Strength Continue to Drive Cash Flow? - The Globe and Mail
content: Suncor Energy Inc. SU continues to benefit from its integrated refining operations, supported by stronger refining margins, high utilization and growing refined product sales. The company's downstream business has become a significant contributor to cash generation, raising expectations about its ability to sustain profitability. In the third quarter of 2026, Suncor's Refining and Marketing segment generated C$3.61 billion in adjusted funds from operations, compared with C$1.22 billion a year earlier. Segment free funds flow increased to C$3.29 billion from C$926 million, reflecting favorable refining conditions. Higher cracking margins were a major contributor to the improvement. Operational performance remained encouraging, with refinery utilization reaching 95% and crude throughput of approximately 488,000 barrels per day. Refined product sales increased to a third-quarter record of nearly 677,000 barrels per day from approximately 647,000 barrels a year earlier. Previous debottlenecking initiatives expanded high-value export capacity, while stronger domestic retail sales supported performance. Suncor's integrated operations provide another advantage. The Edmonton refinery's direct connection to oil sands production improves feedstock flexibility and operational efficiency. This integration helped maintain refinery throughput during planned maintenance, while logistics capabilities largely offset supply disruptions in Eastern Canada. Looking ahead, Suncor's 511,000-barrel-per-day refining network, diverse crude sourcing and access to high-value markets support its cash generation potential. However, sustaining the recent momentum will depend on refining margins, product demand and continued operational reliability. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM also benefited from favorable refining conditions in the third quarter of 2026. The company's Energy Products earnings increased to $7.17 billion from $1.84 billion a year earlier. ExxonMobil achieved 100% crude unit utilization at the U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, reflecting strong operational performance and its ability to capture favorable margins. Chevron Corporation CVX reported downstream earnings of $4.93 billion, compared with $1.14 billion a year earlier, supported by higher refined product margins. The company's U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput of 1.09 million barrels per day, with utilization approaching 98%. Chevron's reliable refining operations highlight its ability to benefit from favorable market conditions. Suncor's shares have gained 67.5% over the past year, outperforming ExxonMobil's 46.3% increase and Chevron's 39.7% rise. SU's stronger share-price performance reflects investor interest in its integrated operations, improved cash generation and shareholder returns. The gains also highlight growing confidence in the company's ability to sustain profitability across its upstream and downstream businesses. Suncor appears attractively valued compared with its integrated energy peers. The stock trades at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 9.59, below ExxonMobil’s 13.26 and Chevron’s 12.45. This suggests that investors can gain exposure to Suncor’s expected earnings at a lower price than those of its larger peers. The valuation discount, combined with solid refining operations and healthy cash generation, adds to the stock’s investment appeal. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Suncor's EPS has increased 18.54% for 2026 and 11.31% for 2027. The current estimates stand at $8.76 per share for 2026 and $7.28 for 2027. These upward revisions indicate improving analyst expectations for Suncor's earnings performance, supported by its integrated business model and favorable operating conditions. Suncor's strong refining performance, growing cash flow and integrated operations support its outlook. The stock’s attractive valuation relative to peers and upward earnings estimate revisions further strengthen its investment appeal, despite refining margin volatility. Instead of relying on the upstream to carry the quarter, the Texas-based company showed that its refining and fuels business can swing the earnings picture in a matter of months. Adjusted earnings were higher than in the prior quarter, operating cash flow was robust, and net debt continued to fall as the balance sheet strengthened further. The release, issued recently, arrives at a moment when energy markets are still processing geopolitical disruption, uneven demand signals and a more cautious tone about the path of crude benchmarks. Readers following oil and gas stocks will recognise that the quarter's story is less about the direction of oil prices than about how a large, diversified operator turns operational reliability into cash. The headline takeaway from the release is a change in the centre of gravity. For several years, the narrative around Exxon Mobil focused on upstream growth, with Guyana and the Permian Basin supplying most of the excitement. In the latest quarter, the energy products division, which houses refining and fuels, produced earnings that more than doubled from the previous quarter and outpaced the upstream segment by a clear margin. That reversal matters because it illustrates why integrated oil companies exist. When crude prices soften, refiners often benefit from cheaper feedstock, provided product prices keep. The company highlighted that crude unit utilisation at its Gulf Coast refineries reached full capacity during the period, alongside strong diesel output. Running plants at that intensity is rarely accidental. It reflects years of maintenance planning, unit upgrades and a deliberate effort to shift yields toward higher-value products such as distillates. The Beaumont refinery expansion is part of that story. The addition of capacity at the Texas site has lifted distillate production along the Gulf Coast meaningfully since the end of the last decade, giving the company more exposure to a product that remains tightly linked to freight, farming and industrial activity. The upstream segment posted lower adjusted earnings than in the previous quarter. Several factors explain most of the move. Lower realised prices weighed on revenue, and an accelerated entitlement effect in Guyana reduced the company's share of production under the terms of the production sharing contract. Entitlement mechanics can confuse casual observers. Under many production sharing agreements, the host government and partners recover costs first, and as those costs are repaid the operator's share of barrels can shift. The accelerated effect in the latest quarter means a portion of the expected shift arrived earlier than modelled, which trims posted earnings without changing the physical flow of oil from the Stabroek block. Despite the sequential decline, the longer-run upstream picture remains favourable on a year-to-date basis. Chemical products earnings declined in the quarter as margins narrowed, even though volumes in Asia Pacific improved. That combination is typical of a commodity chemical cycle in which new capacity in one region pressures pricing while demand growth remains uneven. The segment has been a source of frustration for the sector for some time, and the latest result does not change the tone. Year to date, however, the chemicals business is stronger than it was a year earlier. The company attributes that to record reliability and a wider feedstock advantage in North America, where abundant natural gas liquids give domestic crackers a cost edge over naphtha-based competitors in other regions. Liquefied natural gas projects are capital intensive and slow to develop, often taking many years from discovery to first cargo. They also carry political and logistical risks, particularly in frontier jurisdictions where infrastructure is limited. Structural savings differ from cyclical ones because they persist when prices change. So is that higher profit Exxon’s own, or the market’s? So far, more of it looks like the market’s. Exxon earned $15.4 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, against $7.55 billion a year earlier. The company earned $4.18 billion in fiscal Q1 2026, meaning the whole step up arrived in the last two quarters. Fiscal Q2 2026 profit was already $14.5 billion. Management said a lack of supply led to tight markets and higher prices. Its guess was that fuel markets would not get back closer to normal until well through 2027, or longer. Chevron and ConocoPhillips shares rose by similar amounts on report day, so the quarter did little to set Exxon apart from its peers. Exxon does have gains of its own. Management cited $16.9 billion of structural cost savings since 2019. Setting aside Middle East impacts, executives said production rose from a year earlier, helped by growth in the Permian and Guyana. Those savings accumulated over several years, while the higher profit has lasted just two quarters. Exxon’s payouts hold up so far. The company returned $9.4 billion to holders through dividends and buybacks in fiscal Q3 2026, against $18.5 billion of free cash flow. Management raised the dividend per share 4%, marking its 44th straight year of increases. The company also plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, assuming reasonable market conditions. Exxon carries light debt as well, at 4.9% of its market value against 19.2% for the S&P 500. Profit fell by more than a third, and the payouts kept going. Exxon earned $51.9 billion in the twelve months to September 2022, and $30.0 billion in the twelve months to September 2025. During that leaner year, free cash flow of $23.8 billion landed only a little above the $20.7 billion Exxon spent on buybacks alone. Total payouts of $37.9 billion ran well above free cash flow with $17.2 billion of dividends included. Management said that at the bottom of the cycle, Exxon does not pull back from its commitment to holders and uses the balance sheet to make up the difference. The company has less cash to draw on now, holding $12.2 billion at the end of September 2026, against $30.4 billion four years earlier. Apart from buybacks, management left its 2027 plan to a later date. The company said it will confirm key 2027 planning figures in a press release later in fiscal Q4 2026, offering more detail on its fourth-quarter call in January. Cash flow covered Exxon’s payouts in fiscal Q3 2026, while the company has held its higher profit for only two quarters. Its quarterly profit at the fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch.
